title: Joints: Structure, Innervation, and Function
subject: Musculoskeletal System (MUSC)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains how joints are built, how they are innervated, and how three clinically important joints, the shoulder, knee, and temporomandibular joint, stay stable while they move. Joint classification follows from the tissue between the bones and the shape of the articular surfaces. Hilton law explains joint position sense, protective reflexes, and referred joint pain. Board questions usually describe a mechanism of injury, a positive examination test, a lost movement, or pain felt away from its source, and ask you to name the structure or nerve responsible.
prerequisites: Connective tissue types: dense regular tissue, hyaline cartilage, and fibrocartilage

Muscle actions at the shoulder, hip, knee, and jaw, with their nerve supply
Sensory receptors and the dorsal horn pathways for proprioception and pain
Branches of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3)

connections.how: Avascular articular cartilage depends on synovial fluid for nutrition, which explains why it heals poorly once injured.
Muscles that cross a joint both move it and stabilize it, and their nerves also supply its capsule.
Convergence of joint and skin afferents on shared spinal neurons is the basis of referred joint pain.
Synovium, cartilage, and capsule are the targets of osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, crystal disease, and septic arthritis.
The TMJ shares its nerve supply with the masseter and the skin of the ear and temple, so jaw disease can present as ear pain.

terms.def: A joint that permits essentially no movement, such as a cranial suture.
A joint that permits slight movement, such as the pubic symphysis or an intervertebral disc.
A freely movable joint; all diarthroses are synovial joints.
The vascular connective tissue lining of a joint capsule whose cells secrete hyaluronan and lubricin into synovial fluid.
The number of independent axes about which a joint can rotate: one for a hinge or pivot, two for condyloid and saddle joints, three for a ball and socket.
The nerves supplying the muscles that move a joint also supply the joint capsule and the skin over the muscles' insertions.
Pain perceived at a site other than its source because both sites send afferents to the same spinal cord neurons.
Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis, whose tendons blend with the capsule and press the humeral head into the glenoid.
A fibrocartilage rim attached to the margin of the glenoid fossa that deepens the socket slightly.
Crescent-shaped fibrocartilage pads between the femoral condyles and tibial plateau that improve fit and spread load.
Valgus angulation points the distal segment away from the midline (knee drawn inward); varus points it toward the midline (knee bowed outward).
A plate of dense fibrous tissue or fibrocartilage inside a synovial joint, such as the TMJ, that divides the cavity into two compartments.

sections.title: Classifying joints by function and synovial joints by shape

blocks.text: A joint is any place where two or more bones (or a bone and cartilage) meet. How much it moves depends on what fills the space between the bones. When dense fibrous tissue or cartilage binds the bones directly, the surfaces cannot slide on one another, and motion is absent or slight. When the bones are separated by a fluid-filled cavity enclosed in a capsule, the surfaces are free to move. Two classifications follow from this: a structural one (fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial) and a functional one based on mobility.

blocks.title: Functional classes and the structures that produce them
rows: Fibrous (suture, gomphosis) or primary cartilaginous (synchondrosis of hyaline cartilage)
Cranial sutures, tooth in its socket, epiphyseal growth plate
Secondary cartilaginous (symphysis of fibrocartilage) or a fibrous syndesmosis
Pubic symphysis, intervertebral disc, distal tibiofibular joint
Synovial: capsule, synovial membrane, cavity, articular cartilage
blocks.caption: Every diarthrosis is synovial. Synchondroses are usually temporary and ossify after growth ends.

blocks.text: A synovial joint has a fibrous capsule continuous with the periosteum, an inner synovial membrane that lines everything in the cavity except the articular cartilage, and a thin film of synovial fluid. Synoviocytes secrete hyaluronan, which makes the fluid viscous, and lubricin, which reduces friction at the cartilage surface. Articular cartilage is usually hyaline, has no blood vessels or nerves, and receives its nutrients by diffusion from synovial fluid, aided by the cyclic compression of movement. Some synovial joints (TMJ, sternoclavicular) contain an articular disc, and the knee contains menisci.

Among synovial joints, the shape of the articular surfaces sets the axes of motion. A cylinder in a trough (hinge) or a peg in a ring (pivot) allows rotation about one axis. An oval convex surface in an oval concavity (condyloid, also called ellipsoid) allows flexion, extension, abduction, and adduction but not axial rotation. A saddle joint has two surfaces each convex in one direction and concave in the other, giving two axes. A sphere in a cup (ball and socket) allows three axes, including rotation. Flat surfaces (plane joints) only glide, with motion limited by ligaments.

blocks.title: Synovial joint types
rows: Humeroulnar (elbow), interphalangeal, talocrural (ankle); knee is a modified hinge
Median atlantoaxial (dens in ring of atlas and transverse ligament), proximal radioulnar (radial head in annular ligament)
Flexion, extension, abduction, adduction; opposition with conjunct rotation
All of the above plus medial and lateral rotation
blocks.caption: Number of axes rises with the curvature of the articular surfaces.

blocks.text: Two examples are tested often. At the median atlantoaxial joint the dens of C2 sits in a ring formed by the anterior arch of the atlas and the transverse ligament; the atlas and skull turn around the dens, giving roughly half of cervical rotation. Rupture of the transverse ligament, as in rheumatoid arthritis, lets the dens move back toward the spinal cord. At the first carpometacarpal joint the saddle shape lets the thumb flex across the palm while it rotates medially, so the thumb pad can meet each fingertip in opposition. In general, mobility costs stability: the shallow ball and socket of the shoulder moves most and dislocates most.

sections.title: Hilton law, articular sensation, and referred joint pain

blocks.text: Hilton law states that the nerves supplying the muscles that move a joint also supply the joint itself and the skin over those muscles' insertions. Anatomically, articular branches usually arise from the nerves to nearby muscles as those nerves cross the joint. The muscle, the joint it moves, and the overlying skin therefore share nerves and spinal segments, which lets the joint report its state directly to the reflex circuits that control the muscles around it.

Articular nerves are richest in the fibrous capsule, ligaments, and synovial membrane. Articular cartilage has no nerves, so cartilage loss in osteoarthritis is painless in itself; the pain comes from subchondral bone, synovium, and the stretched capsule. Joint receptors work with muscle spindles to give position and movement sense. Joint receptors signal mainly near the ends of the range, and spindles supply most mid-range position sense.

blocks.title: Articular receptors
rows: Tension near the extremes of motion
Free nerve endings (A-delta and C fibers)
Nociception from stretch, injury, and inflammatory mediators
blocks.caption: Inflammatory mediators such as bradykinin and prostaglandins lower the threshold of joint nociceptors, so normal movement becomes painful.

blocks.text: Because the same afferents feed motor reflexes, capsular stretch or inflammation reflexly inhibits the muscles around the joint. Swelling of the knee, for example, inhibits the quadriceps (arthrogenic muscle inhibition), and a painful joint is held in the position of greatest capsular volume. When articular sensation is lost, as in diabetic neuropathy, tabes dorsalis, or syringomyelia, the joint is repeatedly overloaded without warning and can be destroyed (neuropathic or Charcot joint).

Shared innervation also explains referred pain. The hip capsule is supplied by the femoral nerve anteriorly, the obturator nerve inferomedially, the nerve to quadratus femoris posteriorly, and the superior gluteal nerve superiorly. The femoral and obturator nerves (L2 to L4) also supply the knee and the skin of the anterior and medial thigh. Afferents from the hip and from these skin areas converge on the same dorsal horn neurons, and the brain, more used to signals from skin, projects the pain to the thigh and knee. A child or adolescent with knee pain, such as from slipped capital femoral epiphysis or Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, needs a hip examination.

blocks.title: How hip disease is felt in the knee
steps: Hip capsule is inflamed or stretched
Femoral and obturator nociceptors fire
Afferents enter L2 to L4 dorsal horn
Converge on neurons that also serve thigh and knee
Brain maps the signal to the familiar skin area
Pain is felt in the medial thigh and knee
blocks.caption: Convergence on shared spinal neurons, not nerve damage, produces the referral.

blocks.predict: An obese 13-year-old limps and complains only of left knee pain. The knee examination is normal. Which joint should be examined next, and through which nerves is the pain referred?
blocks.explain: The left hip. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis stretches the hip capsule, and its nociceptive input travels in the obturator and femoral nerves, which also supply the knee and medial thigh, so pain is projected there.

sections.title: Glenohumeral stability, anterior dislocation, and the axillary nerve

blocks.text: The glenohumeral joint is the most mobile joint in the body and the one most often dislocated. Its bony fit is poor: the glenoid fossa is shallow and covers only about a quarter to a third of the humeral head at any moment, and the fibrocartilage labrum deepens it only slightly. The capsule is loose enough to allow wide range, so it is taut only near the extremes of motion. Stability through most of the range therefore comes from muscle rather than from bone or ligament.

blocks.title: Stabilizers of the glenohumeral joint
rows: Deepens the socket and adds a suction seal
Inferior glenohumeral ligament resists anterior translation in abduction and external rotation
Compresses the head into the glenoid; initiates abduction (about 0 to 15 degrees)
Lateral rotation; resists posterior and superior translation
Medial rotation; anterior wall of the joint
blocks.caption: The four cuff tendons blend with the capsule superiorly, anteriorly, and posteriorly, but not inferiorly.

blocks.text: The rotator cuff works by concavity compression. Pulling the humeral head into the glenoid keeps its center fixed while it rotates. This is essential during abduction, because the deltoid's line of pull at low angles would otherwise slide the head upward against the acromion. The cuff and deltoid act as a force couple: the deltoid elevates the arm while the cuff holds the fulcrum in place. A torn cuff therefore causes weakness, superior migration of the head, and impingement even when the deltoid is intact.

The inferior capsule has no cuff tendon over it and is the weakest part of the joint. With the arm abducted and externally rotated, as in blocking a throw or falling on an outstretched hand, the head is levered forward and down through the anteroinferior capsule and comes to rest below the coracoid process. The shoulder looks squared off because the head no longer fills the deltoid beneath the acromion. Anterior dislocation may tear the anteroinferior labrum (Bankart lesion) or impact the posterolateral humeral head on the glenoid rim (Hill-Sachs lesion), both of which favor recurrence. Posterior dislocation is uncommon and classically follows a seizure or electric shock, when the strong medial rotators overpower the lateral rotators.

The axillary nerve (C5, C6, posterior cord) passes through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery and winds around the surgical neck of the humerus, directly below the joint. The displaced head stretches it, as can a fracture of the surgical neck. The result is predictable from what the nerve supplies: the deltoid, teres minor, and skin over the lower deltoid through the superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm. Numbness over this patch is the quickest bedside sign of axillary nerve injury.

blocks.title: Anterior dislocation to axillary nerve palsy
steps: Arm abducted and externally rotated under force
Head levered through weak anteroinferior capsule
Head lies below the coracoid process
Axillary nerve stretched around the surgical neck
Deltoid and teres minor denervated
Weak abduction past 15 degrees; numb lower deltoid skin
blocks.caption: Supraspinatus can still start abduction, and infraspinatus masks most of the lateral rotation loss.

blocks.predict: After reduction of an anterior dislocation, a patient can begin abducting the arm but cannot raise it further, and lateral rotation is only slightly weak. Which nerve is injured, and why is the first part of abduction spared?
blocks.explain: The axillary nerve. Supraspinatus, supplied by the suprascapular nerve, initiates abduction and is intact, but the deltoid, the main abductor from about 15 to 90 degrees, is paralyzed. Infraspinatus, also suprascapular, still performs most lateral rotation, so loss of teres minor is subtle.

sections.title: Knee ligaments, menisci, and the tests that examine them

blocks.text: The knee is a modified hinge: rounded femoral condyles sit on a nearly flat tibial plateau, so bone shape adds little stability, and flexion and extension come with a small amount of rotation. Four main ligaments and two menisci keep it aligned. Each ligament resists one direction of displacement, so each test applies that displacement and looks for excess movement or a soft end point.

The cruciate ligaments lie inside the capsule but outside the synovial cavity and are named for their tibial attachments. The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) runs from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia upward, backward, and laterally to the medial surface of the lateral femoral condyle; it stops the tibia sliding forward on the femur and limits hyperextension. The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL), stronger and thicker, runs from the posterior intercondylar area upward and forward to the lateral surface of the medial femoral condyle; it stops the tibia sliding backward and is the main stabilizer of the flexed, weight-bearing knee. The medial (tibial) collateral ligament is a broad flat band whose deep fibers attach to the capsule and medial meniscus. The lateral (fibular) collateral ligament is a round cord to the fibular head, separated from the lateral meniscus by the popliteus tendon.

blocks.title: Knee structures and their tests
rows: Lachman (knee at 20 to 30 degrees); anterior drawer (90 degrees)
Excess forward glide of the tibia with a soft end point
Valgus force (opening of the medial side)
Varus force (opening of the lateral side)
Load spreading; torn by compression with rotation
Painful click or catch on rotation
blocks.caption: At 20 to 30 degrees of flexion a collateral can be judged alone; gaping in full extension implies cruciate or capsular injury too.

blocks.text: Lachman is more sensitive than the anterior drawer, particularly soon after injury. At 90 degrees, hamstring guarding pulls the tibia back and the posterior horn of the medial meniscus wedges against the femoral condyle, blocking forward glide; at 20 to 30 degrees neither happens.

The menisci are fibrocartilage wedges that deepen the plateau and spread load; only their outer rim is vascular, so inner tears heal poorly. The C-shaped medial meniscus is fixed to the deep MCL and capsule, so it cannot shift away when the femur rotates and compresses it, and the medial compartment also carries more load. The nearly circular lateral meniscus is free of the LCL and is pulled back by popliteus during flexion. The medial meniscus therefore tears more often. Swelling timing helps localize injury: the ACL carries a branch of the middle genicular artery, so its rupture causes hemarthrosis within hours, whereas an isolated meniscal tear swells more slowly.

blocks.title: The unhappy triad from a lateral blow
steps: Blow to lateral knee, foot planted, knee slightly flexed
Valgus force opens the medial side
MCL tears
Continued valgus with rotation ruptures the ACL
Medial meniscus, fixed to the MCL, may also tear
blocks.caption: In noncontact pivoting ACL injuries, the lateral meniscus is often the one torn.

blocks.title: Reading a knee examination
blocks.text: A skier twists a planted knee, hears a pop, and the knee swells within 2 hours. At 25 degrees of flexion the tibia glides forward with no firm end point, while the anterior drawer at 90 degrees is equivocal. Valgus stress at 25 degrees opens the medial joint line. Rapid swelling means a vascular structure bled, most often the ACL, and the positive Lachman confirms it; guarding and the meniscal block masked the drawer. Medial gapping means a torn MCL, and medial joint line tenderness with a painful McMurray would add the medial meniscus.

sections.title: The temporomandibular joint and disc displacement

blocks.text: The temporomandibular joint (TMJ) is a synovial joint between the head (condyle) of the mandible and the mandibular fossa and articular eminence of the temporal bone. Unlike most synovial joints, its articular surfaces are covered by fibrocartilage rather than hyaline cartilage. An articular disc of dense fibrous tissue divides the cavity into two separate synovial compartments. The disc is biconcave, with thick anterior and posterior bands and a thin intermediate zone on which the condyle normally sits. Behind it, a vascular, richly innervated retrodiscal tissue (bilaminar zone) attaches it to the temporal bone and condyle, and in front the superior head of the lateral pterygoid inserts into the disc and capsule. The lateral (temporomandibular) ligament thickens the capsule and limits posterior displacement of the condyle.

blocks.title: The two TMJ compartments
rows: Wide opening, protrusion, and side-to-side grinding
blocks.caption: Wide opening requires both compartments working in sequence.

blocks.title: Opening the mouth at the TMJ
steps: Digastric and other suprahyoid muscles depress the mandible
Condyle rotates under the disc (lower compartment)
Lateral pterygoid pulls condyle and disc forward
Disc and condyle glide onto the eminence (upper compartment)
Full opening; condyle sits under the eminence
blocks.caption: Closing reverses the sequence, driven by temporalis, masseter, and medial pterygoid, with posterior temporalis fibers retracting the condyle.

blocks.text: The joint is supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve, the main supply to the posterior and lateral capsule, and by the masseteric nerve anteriorly, both branches of CN V3. This fits Hilton law: the masseteric nerve supplies the masseter that moves the joint. The auriculotemporal nerve also supplies the skin of the temple, tragus, and external acoustic meatus, so TMJ pain is commonly felt in front of or inside the ear. Because the lateral pterygoids pull the condyles forward, a unilateral CN V3 lesion makes the jaw deviate toward the paralyzed side on opening.

Disc displacement is usually anterior or anteromedial, in the direction of the lateral pterygoid's pull, once the retrodiscal tissue has been stretched. With the disc ahead of the condyle, the condyle rests on the retrodiscal tissue, whose compression and inflammation cause pain. In displacement with reduction, the condyle jumps over the thick posterior band onto the intermediate zone during opening, which produces a click, and the disc slips off again near the end of closing, sometimes with a softer second click (reciprocal clicking). In displacement without reduction, the disc stays in front and blocks forward translation, so the click disappears, opening is limited (closed lock), and the jaw deviates toward the affected side because that condyle cannot glide. Dislocation is different: the condyle itself passes in front of the eminence, often during a yawn, and the mouth is locked open.

blocks.title: Interpreting a click and a lock
blocks.text: A patient has had a painless click on opening the right jaw for months. One morning the click is gone, the mouth opens only partway, and the jaw swings to the right as it opens. Before, the disc was displaced anteriorly but recaptured each time the condyle crossed its posterior band, so the click marked reduction. Now the disc no longer reduces, so it blocks forward gliding of the right condyle. The left condyle still translates, which turns the mandible toward the right. Pain in front of the ear reflects compressed retrodiscal tissue supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve.

integration.text: Anatomy and histology explain how joints fail. Avascular, aneural articular cartilage and the avascular inner menisci heal poorly, so mechanical injury tends to progress to osteoarthritis, while the vascular, innervated synovium, capsule, and retrodiscal tissue are where pain, swelling, and inflammatory arthritis arise. Rheumatoid synovitis loosens ligaments such as the transverse ligament of the atlas, and loss of articular sensation in neuropathy removes the protective reflexes that Hilton law describes, leading to neuropathic joint destruction.

Neuroscience explains the clinical pattern. Joint, muscle, and skin afferents share segments, so the examiner must look beyond the painful region: knee pain may come from the hip, and ear pain from the TMJ. Examination tests are directional reasoning, not memorized lists, but they have limits: guarding, effusion, and combined injuries reduce their accuracy, and imaging confirms what the history and mechanism suggest.

summary: Mobility depends on the tissue between bones: fibrous and cartilaginous joints are synarthroses or amphiarthroses, and all diarthroses are synovial.

Surface shape sets the axes: hinge and pivot one, condyloid and saddle two, ball and socket three, plane joints glide; the median atlantoaxial joint is a pivot and the first carpometacarpal joint a saddle.
Hilton law: nerves to the muscles that move a joint also supply the joint and overlying skin, linking articular sensation to protective muscle reflexes.
Hip pain referred to the knee travels in the femoral and obturator nerves (L2 to L4), which converge with knee and thigh afferents in the dorsal horn.
The shallow glenoid makes the shoulder depend on rotator cuff compression; the uncovered inferior capsule allows anteroinferior dislocation in abduction and external rotation.
Anterior dislocation stretches the axillary nerve: deltoid weakness beyond about 15 degrees of abduction, mild lateral rotation loss, and numbness over the lower deltoid.
ACL and PCL stop anterior and posterior tibial translation (Lachman and anterior drawer; posterior drawer); MCL and LCL resist valgus and varus stress.
The medial meniscus tears more often because its attachment to the MCL and capsule keeps it from moving out of the way.
The TMJ has fibrocartilage surfaces and a disc creating a lower hinge and upper gliding compartment; it is supplied by the auriculotemporal and masseteric branches of CN V3.
Anterior disc displacement with reduction clicks on opening; without reduction it causes closed lock, limited opening, and deviation toward the affected side.

The supraspinatus range for initiating abduction is quoted as 0 to 15 degrees in most texts but up to 0 to 30 degrees in some; confirm the value NABNE uses.
Classification of the radiocarpal and atlanto-occipital joints (condyloid versus ellipsoid) and of the sternoclavicular joint (saddle type) differs slightly among anatomy texts.
The classic unhappy triad lists the medial meniscus; studies of acute ACL injuries report lateral meniscal tears as often or more often. Confirm which version NABNE expects.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Hilton law, Bankart lesion, Hill-Sachs lesion, Lachman, McMurray, and Charcot joint, or only the descriptive terms.
Some texts add deep temporal nerve branches to the TMJ supply; the registry competency names only the auriculotemporal and masseteric nerves.
